GC/MS deconvolution: mathematical basis

Source: vignettes/articles/algorithm.Rmd
algorithm.Rmd

Let Y=(y_{ij})\in\mathbb R_+^{n\times m} contain the observed ion intensities, with scans i=1,\ldots,n in rows and mass channels j=1,\ldots,m in columns. Deconvolution estimates the contributions of individual compounds to the mean signal M=(\mu_{ij}), together with a smooth background. GCMSprime combines grouped sparse regression, PSF estimation and shape-constrained matrix factorization in a common likelihood-based workflow.

Write the weighted observation log likelihood as

\ell_\nu(M;Y)=\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^m w_{ij}\ell_\nu(y_{ij};\mu_{ij}),

where w_{ij}\geq0 are supplied observation weights and \nu contains the noise parameters. For quasipoisson data, the corresponding quasi-likelihood has the Poisson mean-dependent part divided by the estimated dispersion \phi. The same notation below covers likelihood and quasi-likelihood; Section 5 specifies the noise models. The identification article covers retention indices and spectral library search.

1. Deconvolution based on a known peak shape

Suppose the response to a narrow input is a known point spread function (PSF), or peak shape function, g. Shifted copies form the columns of X(g)\in\mathbb R_+^{n\times p}, where p is the number of candidate peak positions. The mean model is

M=X(g)C+BA+O,\qquad C\geq0,\quad A\geq0.

Here C\in\mathbb R_+^{p\times m} contains the ion amplitudes, B\in\mathbb R_+^{n\times q} is a low-dimensional background basis, A contains its coefficients, and O is optional known additive signal. A nonzero row of C calls a peak using evidence from all mass channels. Define its row-support size by

s(C)=\|C\|_{2,0} =\sum_{r=1}^{p}\mathbf 1\{\|C_{r\cdot}\|_2>0\}.

The grouped L_0 selection target is

\mathcal G(C,A;g) =-2\ell_\nu\{X(g)C+BA+O;Y\}+\lambda_g s(C).

The row charge \lambda_g trades improved fit against the number of called peaks; background terms are compulsory and unpenalized. Minimizing this criterion corresponds to best subset of groups selection (BSGS): each group consists of all channel coefficients at one candidate position. It seeks the jointly most parsimonious peak calls supported by the complete multichannel signal.

L0glm approximates this selection problem using iterative adaptive ridge regression within GLM IRLS. The GIC preset supplies the information-criterion scale

\lambda_{\rm IC}=\log p\,\log\log n,

with natural logarithms, as motivated for high-dimensional penalized likelihood by Fan & Tang (2013). The adaptive-ridge calibration uses a quarter of this scale, with the appropriate dispersion factor in the working quadratic. Grouped selection shares support information across channels; a relaxed fit then re-estimates the amplitudes on the selected rows. The total compound charge used by GCMSprime’s final factorization is specified in Section 3.

The sparse pulse-train formulation was inspired by de Rooi & Eilers (2011). Our extensions add an efficient information-criterion regularization preset, grouped selection approximating BSGS, and likelihood-based treatment of Poisson or overdispersed Poisson ion-intensity noise. In the overdispersed case, the selection target is the corresponding quasi-GIC, with the estimated variance scale retained in the quasi-likelihood. This is especially useful for electron-multiplier measurements, whose variation exceeds that of ideal ion counts.

2. Estimate an unknown or time-varying PSF

When g is unknown, the convolution model is bilinear in g and C. For a fixed channel spike train c_j=C_{\cdot j},

X(g)c_j=T(c_j)g,

where T(c_j) contains shifted copies of c_j. Thus both conditional subproblems can be expressed as nonnegative GLMs. Blind PSF estimation alternates two L0glm fits:

  1. Spike-train update: hold g fixed and estimate C,A from Y using grouped sparse regression on [X(g),B].
  2. PSF update: hold the spike trains fixed and regress informative ion traces on T(c_j), with the background and known signal in the offset. The current kernel is the ridge prior center; positive starts preserve eligible tails. Combine the channel estimates, impose the kernel shape constraint, align its centroid and normalize its sum to one.

These are alternating block-coordinate updates for the joint sparse likelihood target

\mathcal G(C,A,g) =-2\ell_\nu\{X(g)C+BA+O;Y\}+\lambda_g s(C),

subject to nonnegativity and a normalized, log-concave kernel. The second block uses adaptive ridge regularization and shape smoothing to stabilize kernel estimation. Completed kernel proposals are compared after refitting their spike trains and backgrounds with the requested information criterion; the best synchronized checkpoint is retained. This makes the criterion apply to the complete reconstructed signal. The numerical procedure uses approximate conditional updates rather than exact minimization of each block.

The same observation model is carried through both fits. With the default quasipoisson model, the pooled dispersion is estimated first and reused as a fixed inverse-variance scale. Poisson sets \phi=1; the other supported noise families use their corresponding likelihoods. An alkane standard with isolated peaks can provide the initial kernel, followed by blind refinement on the sample.

For a time-varying PSF, repeat the local estimation in overlapping windows centered at \tau_1<\cdots<\tau_R. Between adjacent anchors, interpolate the log kernels and renormalize:

g_t=\frac{\exp\{(1-a)\log g_r+a\log g_{r+1}\}} {\sum_\ell\exp\{(1-a)\log g_{r\ell}+a\log g_{r+1,\ell}\}}, \qquad 0\leq a\leq1.

Convex combinations of concave log profiles preserve log-concavity. Each candidate peak receives the interpolated shape for its retention region, giving a sparse, time-varying convolution design. The full-chromatogram default uses ten PSF anchors. See PSF estimation in L0nmf for the calibration and windowed-estimation algorithms.

3. Compound- and concentration-dependent PSFs

A time-varying common PSF captures instrumental drift, while compound chemistry and concentration can produce additional broadening, tailing or overload. To accommodate these effects, each compound receives its own profile in the factorization

\mu_{ij}=\sum_{r=1}^{K}H_{ir}S_{rj}+(BA)_{ij}+O_{ij}, \qquad H,S,A\geq0.

The columns of H are elution profiles and the rows of S are mass spectra. Each profile has unit sum and a contiguous positive support, with

\Delta^2\log H_{\cdot r}\leq0.

On an equally spaced scan grid this is equivalent, at interior positive ordinates, to H_{ir}^2\geq H_{i-1,r}H_{i+1,r}. For an irregular time grid, the successive slopes of the log profile must be nonincreasing.

Log-concavity accommodates a broad range of chromatographic shapes: Gaussian peaks, exponentially modified Gaussian peaks, and asymmetric triangular or shark-fin-shaped acid peaks. Gaussian and exponential profiles are log-concave, and their convolution remains log-concave; this gives the exponentially modified Gaussian case. See Saumard & Wellner (2014) for the closure properties. Log-concavity implies unimodality and additionally constrains the evolution of the rising and falling slopes. It therefore provides stronger shape information than the unimodality constraint commonly used in MCR-ALS, helping prevent shoulders and fragments from being assigned to a single incoherent component. The MCR-ALS framework and its constraints are reviewed by de Juan, Jaumot & Tauler (2014).

The rank-selection objective is

J(H,S,A,K) =-2\ell_\nu(HS+BA+O;Y)+\lambda_RK, \qquad \lambda_R=m\kappa\lambda_{\rm IC}.

Here m is the original number of mass channels and \kappa=1 for independent observations; an optional temporal-correlation adjustment is described in Section 5. Equivalently, dividing by m gives -2\ell_\nu/m+\kappa\lambda_{\rm IC}K, with one rank-selection charge per compound. Smooth background coefficients and profile complexity receive no additional penalty under this compound-count convention. Reported IC values use mK plus the number of estimated shared noise parameters as their complexity count.

For fixed K, local conditional likelihood fits refine the spectra, profiles and background. For example, updating compound r uses

\mu_{ij}=R^{(-r)}_{ij}+H_{ir}S_{rj}, \qquad R^{(-r)}=BA+O+\sum_{s\ne r}H_{\cdot s}S_{s\cdot},

so the remaining fitted signal is an offset. Only the affected scan window needs updating. A constrained quadratic step in \log H_{\cdot r} uses the original intensity likelihood and is checked by backtracking. This preserves the chosen noise model while imposing a hard shape constraint. The spectra serve as covariates for the time profiles, with current profiles and spectra supplying the starting values. The native solver refines one log profile at a time and jointly refits the overlapping spectra. Fine refinement has no additional shrinkage toward zero or toward the starting peak shape. It normalizes each updated profile and transfers its scale to the spectrum, preserving the fitted contribution. The model belongs to the broader class of deviance matrix factorization and generalized matrix factorization models, with additional nonnegativity, log-concavity and rank selection.

4. Automatically estimate the true number of compounds present

The number of compounds is estimated together with their profiles and spectra. Grouped deconvolution with the estimated time-varying PSF first supplies a statistically grounded set of candidate components. An unusually broad or tailed compound can initially produce several nearby components; spectral similarity identifies plausible fragments of the same compound.

The starting search uses an unadjusted IC preset to retain a useful pool of candidate components while their shapes are being refined. Final rank selection then applies the requested working-correlation multiplier \kappa. The initialization and final criterion have separate ledgers when their penalties differ.

The algorithm then proposes fusions of correlated spectra whose profiles overlap and whose combined elution profile is compatible with log-concavity. Local profile and spectral refinement assesses each proposal under the rank-selection objective. Unsupported components can be deleted, and residual-supported components can be added. For a move from K to K', acceptance is based on

\Delta J=-2\{\ell_\nu(M';Y)-\ell_\nu(M;Y)\} +\lambda_R(K'-K)\leq0,

up to numerical tolerance. The noise parameters and numerical rank penalty are held fixed during these comparisons. This balances explanatory power against the number of compounds, yielding an automatically selected factorization rank and a data-driven estimate of the underlying compound count.

For a small fragment contained within a broad peak, spectral similarity can be informative even when the two profile shapes differ substantially. The final pass considers fragments with spectral cosine at least 0.97, at least 99% of their profile mass inside the broad parent’s 1%-height interval, and at most 15% of its area. The parent’s FWHM must exceed four times the calibrated narrow-peak FWHM. A proposed merge and an unmerged control receive the same local joint-refinement budget. All original ion channels enter the decision. The other fitted components and background remain in an offset, and local windows include the entire support of each component whose spectrum changes.

The distinctive contribution is the combination of grouped sparse PSF-based initialization, noise-aware log-concave refinement and explicit compound-count selection within one objective-driven workflow. It extends conventional fixed-rank MCR-ALS formulations by selecting the rank during refinement. Automatic component determination also appears in other GC/MS approaches, including ADAP-GC 4.0; here it is integrated with the rank-penalized, shape-constrained likelihood.

For speed, initialization and fusion can aggregate ion traces into at most 32 size-adjusted groups. The compound charge retains the original m, and final refinement and acceptance checks use every original channel. Thus the fitted spectra retain low-abundance diagnostic ions. The L0nmf mathematical article gives the precise initialization, constrained solvers and pseudocode.

5. Modelled smooth background and flexible noise models

A low-dimensional nonnegative B-spline basis represents the smooth background BA. Its coefficients are compulsory, unpenalized terms and are fitted conditionally on the compound signal. The basis is deliberately much smoother than an individual peak: full chromatograms can follow slow baseline drift, while short windows can use a constant background. A lower-quantile background estimate initializes calibration peak detection.

EI mass-spectrometric intensities commonly exhibit overdispersed counting variation. Ion arrivals are approximately Poisson, while the stochastic gain of the electron multiplier adds variation to the recorded intensity. In a simple compound-Poisson representation,

Y=\sum_{a=1}^{N}G_a,\quad N\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\Lambda), \qquad \operatorname{E}(Y)=\Lambda\operatorname{E}(G),\quad \operatorname{Var}(Y)=\Lambda\operatorname{E}(G^2).

Consequently, variance is proportional to the mean, with a scale determined by detector gain and the intensity units. This motivates an overdispersed Poisson working model for GC/MS electron-multiplier signals; additional electronics and digitization can also contribute noise. See Ipsen (2015) for a physical derivation of mass-spectral intensity variation.

The default is therefore quasipoisson with estimated dispersion: \operatorname{Var}(Y_{ij})=\phi\mu_{ij}, implemented as family=quasipoisson("identity"). With \widehat\phi fixed, the mean-dependent quasi-likelihood is

Q(M;Y)=\frac{1}{\widehat\phi} \sum_{ij}w_{ij}\{y_{ij}\log\mu_{ij}-\mu_{ij}\}.

Thus quasi-GIC comparisons use Poisson deviance divided by \widehat\phi, together with the same compound-count penalty. The package reports these quasi-criteria through its regular IC methods.

Seven identity-link signal models are available:

Model Conditional variance or observation convention
Gaussian \sigma^2
Poisson \mu
Quasipoisson \phi\mu
Negative binomial, NB2 \mu+\mu^2/\theta
Negative binomial, NB1 \phi\mu, with \phi\geq1
Gamma \phi\mu^2; zeros are left-censored below the specified detection limit
Common-scale Gamma b_0\mu for the latent signal, with the same censoring convention

Noise parameters are pooled across channels. Fourth- and eighth-order temporal differences suppress the smooth signal and estimate marginal variation; their relationship also supports a lag-one covariance estimate. GCMSprime reuses the calibrated noise specification for PSF estimation and factorization. This keeps candidate-rank comparisons on a common noise scale. An optional negative NB2 theta start permits subsequent likelihood-based updates as documented in L0nmf.

For temporally correlated scan noise, the working information adjustment \kappa=1+2\widehat\rho_1 increases the rank charge. The marginal variance remains in the observation model. Pearson residuals use that marginal mean-variance relationship, allowing residual heatmaps to compare strong and weak ion channels on a common scale.

6. Integrate and inspect each sample

With \sum_iH_{ir}=1, S_{rj} is the discrete integrated intensity of ion j in compound r. The total-intensity profile is P_{ir}=H_{ir}\sum_jS_{rj}, and the normalized spectrum is T_{rj}=S_{rj}/\sum_jS_{rj}, preserving HS=PT. GCMSprime reports both discrete totals and time-weighted integrated areas, alongside sample names, retention times, widths and compound IDs. Profiles and spectra are ordered by apex retention time by default.

Trace plots overlay fitted compounds on background-corrected observed ion traces. Heatmaps show observations, corrected observations, fitted signal and Pearson residuals. Profile/spectrum panels show the recovered shapes and ion patterns. The single-sample tutorial demonstrates the CDF workflow and MSP, Excel and PDF outputs.

7. Analyze samples together

Across samples, retention times drift and a compound can vary in width, tailing and abundance or be entirely absent. Coupled factorization starts from individual-sample fits and estimates a shared spectrum for matched occurrences while retaining sample-specific profiles, areas and backgrounds.

High-confidence spectral matches supply alignment anchors. Each anchor is the leading 1%-height crossing plus half the width of a small peak in that region, reducing tail-related timing shifts. A robust, smooth monotone map captures retention-time drift, with concentration-related anchor motion accounted for separately.

Candidate matches must agree in spectral shape and aligned time. Comparing their profiles in area order checks compatibility with a coherent log-concave ridge across samples. Shared spectra are refined using pooled evidence from their occurrences. The coupled criterion counts a shared spectrum once and each detected occurrence’s amplitude separately.

Alignment retains each sample’s measured scan grid. Profile coordinates and bin widths transform with an area-preserving Jacobian. Known exposure can be supplied for integrated-count measurements; the default unit exposure preserves vendor intensity units.

Observations and factor checkpoints are stored per sample on disk. Updates read one sample at a time while keeping shared spectra and compact matching summaries in memory. Local retention-time comparisons avoid an all-pairs occurrence-distance matrix. Samples retain acquisition order and group labels; alkane standards are selected by acquisition time. Missing occurrences are reported as NA.

See multiple-sample deconvolution for the directory workflow and L0nmf’s coupled model for its objective and mathematical specification.

8. Identify the recovered compounds

GCMSprime imports open and commercial spectral libraries. Alkane-derived retention indices first restrict candidate identities to compounds compatible with the selected stationary phase and RI tolerance. Spectral similarity then ranks those candidates. Consensus IDs connect repeated occurrences to a unique-compound summary across the experiment.

Retention indices and spectral identification describes diagnostic-ion alkane assignments, calibration, column classes, spectral distances and ion weighting. The library-search tutorial gives executable calls and annotated exports.

Parallel processing and sample-specific peak shapes

Directory analyses use one total logical-core budget. For example, ncores=16L uses sixteen single-threaded sample workers when at least sixteen chromatograms are available. With fewer samples, each worker receives a larger share of the native thread budget. Every sample retains its own sparse PSF, scan grid, background and noise calibration.

A shared aggregation is learned from summed chromatograms in common time bins. Matching and Poisson/quasipoisson profile proposals use these ion groups; proposal acceptance and spectral estimation use the original mass channels. The common grid is used only to learn the groups. Original observations are stored on disk, aggregate matrices are cached in RAM, and original-channel updates read bounded blocks. Each worker receives its assigned sample and compact factors.

With shared spectra fixed, profiles and backgrounds can be updated independently across samples. Spectral contributions are then pooled in acquisition order. The spectral fusion queue retains unaffected candidates and refreshes only edges incident to a merged compound, preserving the greedy selection rule. These execution details and the complete objective are given in the L0nmf algorithm.
